title: Harry Houdini Died 100 Years Ago This Halloween: Was He Really Killed by a Punch to the Stomach?
description:
in History |   	October 26th, 2026  Leave a Comment

body:
in History |   	October 26th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

This Hal­loween marks the 100th anniver­sary of the death of famed escape artist Har­ry Hou­di­ni. Today, most of us know more about the man­ner of that death than we do about any of the feats of escape artistry that made him famous in the first place. As the sto­ry goes, he’d mas­tered his own body to the extent that he could tight­en his abdom­i­nal mus­cles so as to with­stand even the hard­est punch to the gut. Or at least that’s the image he let cir­cu­late: tak­ing it as a chal­lenge, a stu­dent and ama­teur box­er turned up and offered his fist to Hou­di­ni as an unex­pect­ed test. A week and a half lat­er, the great escapol­o­gist was dead of peri­toni­tis.
It seemed that the blow he sus­tained had rup­tured Hou­dini’s already-inflamed appen­dix, and that remained the wide­ly accept­ed, if not med­ical­ly air­tight, expla­na­tion for near­ly a cen­tu­ry. Yet there was always some­thing too dra­mat­i­cal­ly neat in the tale of a man famed for defy­ing death being done in by noth­ing more than a thought­less young man’s suck­er punch. Gen­er­a­tions of enthu­si­asts have offered expla­na­tions of their own, some more plau­si­ble than oth­ers, but few inves­ti­ga­tions into this qua­si-leg­endary demise have been con­duct­ed as seri­ous­ly as the one under­tak­en in our time by retired urol­o­gist Lar­ri­an Gille­spie, author of Hou­di­ni: The Man Who Died Twice.
When she had the chance to exam­ine his death cer­tifi­cate, Gille­spie noticed appar­ent irreg­u­lar­i­ties that led her down the rab­bit hole to “a paper trail of mis­state­ments and actions by more than a dozen peo­ple close to Hou­di­ni, includ­ing rel­a­tives and employ­ees,” writes the New York Times’ Robin Pogre­bin, “includ­ing a con­spir­a­cy to change his offi­cial death date to Octo­ber 31st, fix­ing his mem­o­ry to Hal­loween.” Accord­ing to her recon­struc­tion of events, Hou­di­ni actu­al­ly died the day before: not of appen­dici­tis, and not as a result of the young man’s punch. “Rather, she argues, the cul­prit was a bow­el obstruc­tion, brought on by a fibrous mass of chop suey that Hou­di­ni ate on Oct. 28.”


	

Emer­gency surgery took place the next day, but it was too late. “Sep­tic shock set in, Houdini’s fever spiked to 105 and his rapid breath­ing led to mus­cle spasms and uncon­scious­ness.” He was oper­at­ed on again the day after, and “Gillespie’s research into the death cer­tifi­cates indi­cates that the magi­cian died that after­noon at 1:26 p.m.” Gille­spie argues that the lack of a prop­er autop­sy helped con­ceal pos­si­ble med­ical mal­prac­tice and allowed Hou­dini’s wid­ow to col­lect a dou­ble-indem­ni­ty pay­ment for what was treat­ed as an acci­den­tal death. Even if accept­ed, her the­o­ry prob­a­bly won’t erase the cul­tur­al link between Hou­di­ni and Hal­loween. But the the­o­ry does add a new dimen­sion of irony to his life sto­ry: the man who could sur­vive a Chi­nese water tor­ture cell proved to be no match for Amer­i­can Chi­nese food.

body:
in Comics/Cartoons, Music |   	October 26th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Ray Ellis had a six-decade career as a pro­duc­er, arranger, and jazz com­pos­er. And while he’s best known for arrang­ing music for Bil­lie Hol­i­day’s Lady in Satin (1958), he also enjoyed a long career orches­trat­ing music for tele­vi­sion. Work­ing under a pseu­do­nym “Yvette Blais” (his wife’s name), Ellis com­posed back­ground music for the car­toon stu­dio Fil­ma­tion between 1968 and 1982. And, dur­ing the late 60s, he notably cre­at­ed the back­ground and inci­den­tal music for the orig­i­nal Spi­der-Man car­toons.
Above, hear Ray Ellis’ Spi­der-Man sound­track. The show’s talk­ing parts and sound effects have been removed as much as pos­si­ble, then “pieced back togeth­er into com­plete form,” by a YouTu­ber who uses the moniker “11db11.” All of the music from Sea­son 1 is includ­ed, plus many record­ings from Sea­sons 2 and 3. It’s worth not­ing that the 52 episodes from the orig­i­nal 1967 Spi­der-Man TV series have been com­plete­ly restored. You can pur­chase them on DVD online.
Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2017.

title: Scott Kahn Invokes Dreams and Liminality in Atmospheric Landscape Paintings
description: Until a few years ago, painter Scott Kahn was living in his cousin’s attic, with a studio filled with work that he hadn’t had a lot of luck sellin
body:
Until a few years ago, painter Scott Kahn was living in his cousin’s attic, with a studio filled with work that he hadn’t had a lot of luck selling. Then, he began a chance correspondence with the late Canadian artist Matthew Wong, who related to Kahn’s own self-taught background and interest in magical realism. “Matthew was really a great champion of my work,” Kahn told Artnet News. “The only way I can explain it is that we were soulmates.” When Wong’s career took off in 2018, Kahn’s atmospheric, often surreal landscapes also found their audience.
Mostly working in oil on linen, Kahn creates scenes that glow beneath the bright moon or complement architectural elements seen through vignettes of trees and clouds. The works shown here were recently on view in the artist’s sweeping solo exhibition, Silent Night at David Zwirner.
“Berkshire Nightscape II” (2005), oil on linen, 36 1/8 x 40 inches
We encounter nods to American regionalism, such as in “Berkshire Nightscape II” with its pronounced resemblance to Grant Wood’s bulbous, cultivated hills of rural Iowa. Other works invoke the realm of the unconscious, such “The Basement Window,” which recalls a recurring dream the artist has of his childhood home. Trees appear both inside and outside, blurring the boundary between architectural space and nature. In “The Stoop,” a mysterious, deep-forest darkness infringes upon the sunniness of front steps.
In “The Basement,” there is also a subtle connection to the interiority of the body in the trees’ vein-like branches and roots. Through structural apertures, such as a window or a balcony—including the paintings’ inherent frames—the surrounding environment is open to us but always limited. There is always a compelling edge, horizon, shadow, or disappearing path that prompts us to question whether we can truly comprehend what we see.
Kahn’s compositions often feel familiar, yet through deep contrasts, long shadows, nighttime scenes, and portal-like framing, he invokes a sense of enigma and liminality. The scenes are often stretched, as if seen through a wide-angle lens, and there is an indelible sense of transition, whether from night to day, sleeping to waking, or imagination to reality. “I don’t get too bogged down in what a landscape actually is,” Kahn says. “It’s more a vehicle to express a mood. That, to me, is the value of a landscape.”
See more on the artist’s Instagram.
“Leap from the Balcony” (2003), oil on linen, 61 7/8 x 72 inches
“The Stoop” (2024/2025), oil on wood panel, 28 x 22 inches
“The Basement” (2025), oil on linen, 52 1/4 x 60 1/4 inches
“New Moon” (2008/2013), oil on linen, 18 x 20 inches

title: Dreamy Digital Illustrations by Rebecca Zwanzig Tap into Art History and Nostalgia
description: From the atmospheric tones of the Pacific Northwest to Victorian-era textile patterns to antique dishware designs, Rebecca Zwanzig—the artist behi
body:
From the atmospheric tones of the Pacific Northwest to Victorian-era textile patterns to antique dishware designs, Rebecca Zwanzig—the artist behind High West Wild—draws on a wide range of influences. “I grew up in the bluegrass state of Kentucky, and some of my earliest visual memories come from going to auctions and estate sales with my grandma in rural Kentucky,” the artist tells Colossal. “I was always drawn to the patterns on old plates, the embroidery on tablecloths, vintage textiles, and all of these little objects and keepsakes that had clearly belonged to someone and had a life before they ended up there.”
Currently based in Portland, Oregon, by way of Washington’s mountains and Nevada’s desert, the artist draws on this nostalgia in her digital works. Reminiscent of late 19th and early 20th-century motifs, her botanicals emerge from associations with landscapes she has lived in and influences from the not-so-distant past.
“Anna-Marie”
“I’ve always loved vintage textiles and illustration, scientific botanical art, folk art, and the groovy typography and design from the ’60s and ’70s,” Zwanzig says. “My colors tend to come from that same place, too. Lots of earthy 1970s tones…I love anything dark and moody, but I also love really bright, saturated color, so I tend to move between the two.”
Zwanzig’s illustrations often incorporate symmetry and the satisfying repetition of patterns, evoking Art Nouveau and the Arts and Crafts Movement exemplified by the likes of William Morris. Portraits of insects, crystals, and shells, and other natural phenomena also bring to mind natural history tomes such as Lorenz Oken’s Allgemaine Naturgeschichte Für Alle Stände or The Hudson Transparencies.
Her practice developed around early interests in graphic design and oil painting, which she still turns to occasionally to explore the texture of the analog medium. Even her digital pieces created in Procreate or Adobe Illustrator are derived from sketches she first makes by hand to compose lush gradients we associate with oil.
Clients including Starbucks, Marine Layer, Anna Sui, Free People, and more have licensed Zwanzig’s work, and she’s currently in the midst of a personal project of designing a complete tarot deck. If you’re in Seattle next month, you can see Zwanzig’s work at the Renegade Craft Fair, which runs from November 20 to 22. Follow updates and see more from her on the High West Wild Instagram.

title: Giant Ofrenda Arrives in Manhattan Ahead of Día de Muertos
description:
News
                Designed by artisans from Mestiz Studio in Mexico, the public altar welcomes passersby to make offerings to
body:
News
                Designed by artisans from Mestiz Studio in Mexico, the public altar welcomes passersby to make offerings to their loved ones. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            Digital rendering of the ofrenda in Flatiron's North Plaza (all images courtesy Mestiz Studio and Flatiron NoMad Partnership)An enormous ofrenda, titled "Twenty Petal Flower," begins blossoming in Flatiron's North Plaza in Manhattan today, October 26, six days before the start of Día de Muertos (Day of the Dead). Inspired by the terms for the Mexican marigold in Nahuatl (cempōhualxōchitl) and Spanish (cempasúchil), "Twenty Petal Flower" functions as a public community altar where participants can place offerings, candles, gifts, and mementos of their loved ones through November 3. In partnership with Powerhouse Arts in Brooklyn, artisans from Mestiz Studio in Mexico's San Miguel de Allende wove the tiered arrangement into enlarged marigolds, which are thought to help guide the souls of the deceased back to their living family members each year."A Día de Muertos altar is traditionally a tribute to someone we love who is no longer with us. With Twenty Petal Flower, we wanted to honor the people behind the cempasúchil’s entire journey, from cultivation to the ofrenda," Daniel Valero, founder and creative director of Mestiz, told Hyperallergic. An artisan weaves together one of the altar parts.

title: Mamdani Votes Early at The Met. What Other NYC Museums Are Polling Sites?
description:
News
                "It only took five minutes," said the NYC mayor in a social media video. More museums and cultural institut
body:
News
                "It only took five minutes," said the NYC mayor in a social media video. More museums and cultural institutions across the city serve as early voting sites. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Mayor Zohran Mamdani holds up a voting pen in The Met (courtesy NYC Mayor's Office via YouTube) 
    
        
            As New Yorkers line up to cast their midterm ballots early through Sunday, November 1, and others prepare to brave the crowds next Tuesday, November 3, some cultural institutions and museums are turning into voting sites."Only in New York City can you vote in places like the Metropolitan Museum of Art," Mayor Zohran Mamdani reminded viewers in an Instagram video today, October 26, while weaving through The Met's Michael C. Rockefeller Wing at the Manhattan institution. "I just voted here on the first day of early voting. It only took five minutes." Along with hundreds of public schools, community centers, libraries, and other city gathering spaces, several museums are opening their doors for early voters. The American Museum of Natural History in Manhattan will welcome early voters through its 77th Street entrance, according to a banner on its website. Since the 2024 election cycle, the museum has set up voting stations on the first floor of the building for easy accessibility. Across Central Park, The Met returns as an early voting site after serving as one for multiple past general elections and the primaries this June. The Brooklyn Museum, another longtime venue for elections, will also be open for early voting.

title: Nathan Fielder Is a Performance Artist in Disguise
description:
Film Review
                “You Can See Everything” is toted as a documentary, but is Fielder a performance artist playing a do
body:
Film Review
                “You Can See Everything” is toted as a documentary, but is Fielder a performance artist playing a documentarian?
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Still from You Can See Everything (2026), dir. Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim (image courtesy A24)
    
        
            Editor’s Note: This review contains spoilers.As an art historian, it's hard not to relate what you see in everyday life to history — not in the sense that every lily pad recalls Monet or snowballs bring David Hammons to mind, but in the sense that sometimes art really does imitate life. This happened to me recently, maybe 10 minutes into Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s You Can See Everything. I watched Fielder hold painful, prolonged eye contact with Elizabeth Holmes, the convicted fraudster whose eerily large blue eyes seem to enact their own kind of performance. Naturally, I thought of Marina Abramović’s “The Artist is Present” (2010). Perhaps it’s an obvious, pretentious comparison. But hear me out: Is Fielder a documentarian, or is he a performance artist playing one? Artist Martha Wilson recently defined performance art as an intervention that unfolds in real time, often placing the artist’s body at the center of the action. The genre has long tested the limits of what an artist’s body can do, and what an audience will tolerate: Chris Burden had himself shot with a .22-caliber gun in “Shoot” (1971); Yoko Ono invited audience members to cut away her clothing in “Cut Piece” (1964); and Carolee Schneemann pulled a scroll from her vagina in “Interior Scroll” (1975). These works differ considerably, but each makes the artist’s actions and the responses they provoke central to the work. Installation image of "Marina Abramović: The Artist is Present" (2010) (photo Johnathan Muzikar, courtesy the Museum of Modern Art)Fielder, too, puts himself in the middle of things. In You Can See Everything, he spends 34 days filming and questioning Holmes, her partner Billy Evans, and their two children. Eventually, he moves into the guesthouse of their California beachfront rental, just before Holmes begins her 11-year prison sentence for defrauding investors and patients of Theranos, whose blood-testing technology falsely claimed it could run a wide range of tests on a few drops of blood. The couple frames their participation as an act of “radical transparency,” hoping to persuade the public that Holmes is innocent. They chose Fielder as their documentarian, they explain, because he “thinks outside the box” just like they do. Game recognizes game.Fielder’s move turns observation into participation. His proximity to the family becomes part of the experiment, shaping the behavior he records. In one scene, he films himself lurking at a distance as Billy and Holmes embrace. In another, he sits close to Holmes on a couch; a hand strokes her shoulder, and for a moment it seems to belong to Fielder, until the camera reveals Billy on the other side. But the film invites us to imagine a silent intimacy growing between Holmes and Fielder that it never confirms. Elsewhere, Holmes texts flirtatiously, “fyi you can totally see everything.” The title begins to feel less like a promise of transparency and more like provocation: Who is watching who? What does each person want seen?
